newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan finance minister backs off from alliance deal.
newsitem.headline: Japan finance minister backs off from alliance deal.

text.p: Japan's new finance minister has said he might back off from an agreement his party sealed with its alliance partners in exchange for support to re-elect Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
And in a sign of further trouble, the leader of the main opposition party on Saturday launched his first attack against Hashimoto's long-term plan to streamline government bureaucracy.
In two newspaper interviews published on Saturday, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka downplayed the need for creating an independent watchdog agency to oversee financial institutions.

The plan for the watchdog agency, to be independent of the Finance Ministry, was a pillar of the policy deal struck between Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party.

Hashimoto's LDP lacks a majority in both houses of parliament and needs the votes of his alliance partners to push through legistlation. He won re-election on the strength of the loose alliance and formed an all-LDP cabinet on Thursday.
The LDP failed to renew the ruling coalition, and the old allies instead sealed the policy agreement without sending its lawmakers to the new Hashimoto cabinet.
Asked about the alliance agreement on the watchdog agency, the daily Yomiuri Shimbun quoted Mitsuzuka as saying "I won't bother much about that."
Mitsuzuka indicated that the new agency, which would be given powers to probe and oversee banks and other financial institutions, might still be linked to the Finance Ministry.

"My basic idea is that it should be an effective body with necessary powers" that does not require a completely independent status, Mitsuzuka said in a second interview with the leading economic journal, Nihon Keizai Shimbun.

Mitsuzuka's remarks were the first signs of possible backsliding on alliance promises by the new Hashimoto administration, and could raise fears about the cooperation between the LDP, the Social Democrats and Sakigake.

On Saturday, Ichiro Ozawa, chief of the main opposition party Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), launched an attack on Hashimoto's announced timetable for central government reforms, a key plank of his new government.

Hashimoto on Friday said his administration would draft a bill to streamline the 20 central government ministries and agencies by next November, submit the bill for enactment by June 1998 and seek its full implementation by January 2001.
"Doesn't this timetable mean that the government would actually do nothing?" Ozawa told a television talk show on Saturday.

Asked if he would cooperate with the government over reforms, Ozawa said: "We are ready to cooperate over any issue that would be for the nation. But how can we do that when the government has shown us nothing?"
